title: Kula Disaster Recovery Update Meeting: December 5, 2023

recap.headline: Kula fire recovery update: debris cleanup, soil rescrapes, lead screening, test results
recap.in_60_seconds: The Maui Emergency Management Agency hosted its weekly Kula disaster recovery meeting at Kula Elementary with the Mayor, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, the State Department of Health and FEMA. The Corps reported 21 rights of entry, 14 lots cleared, and one closeout package returned to the County; it aims to finish most debris removal by the week of December 18. Three of the soil-sampled lots need another scrape, and waivers are being worked out with owners. Health officials offered lead screening and Tdap shots and said early air sampling found no asbestos and metals below screening levels. About eight residents spoke, pressing for public posting of test results, help for neighbors of contaminated lots, broader health testing, door-to-door schedule notices, and a water line problem that could leave homes without fire protection. Several questions, including when results will be posted and who will help neighbors of contaminated lots, were left for follow-up.

parts.title: Welcome and agenda
presented: The meeting was moved from last week because of a Kona low storm.
Format: updates from MEMA, the Mayor, the Army Corps, the Department of Health and FEMA, then questions.

parts.title: MEMA update
presented: The State Insurance Commissioner was asked about residents' insurance questions and may attend next week.
MEMA is checking how the Department of Education did wipe testing in Lahaina and whether it could work at the Kula site.
Lahaina reentry should finish next week, ending the response phase and moving to recovery.
The former MEMA administrator's contract ended; the speaker is acting administrator until a new one is hired.

next.what: State Insurance Commissioner expected to attend
Department of Education expected to report on wipe testing

parts.title: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers debris update
parts.presenter: Army Corps debris specialist and Recovery Field Office commander
presented: 21 rights of entry so far, with 3 more possibly coming; debris removed from 14 lots.
Soil sampling done on 14 lots, validated results on 10; one complete closeout package returned to the County for permitting.
Goal is to finish most debris removal the week of December 18, followed by sampling, hydroseeding and final sign-off.
A debris call center runs seven days a week, 6:30 a.m. to 6:30 p.m.

next.what: Most debris removal in Kula completed

parts.title: Mayor's remarks
presented: Thanked Kula residents for helping shape the cleanup method.
The County is setting up a new Office of Recovery to help speed rebuilding for those ready to build.

parts.title: Department of Health update
parts.presenter: State Department of Health director and deputy director for environmental health
presented: Lead screening and Tdap shots offered tonight and next week, mainly recommended for children and pregnant women.
Preliminary air sampling found no asbestos, and heavy metals were below screening action levels; results will go on the department's website.
Yellow or orange air sensor readings in Kula were traced to wood chipping, smoking meat and fish, a fireplace and a small yard fire.
State Health and EPA water staff will tour with the County, and Clean Water staff will review stormwater practices for the rainy season.

next.what: Lead screening and Tdap shots offered again
State Health and EPA water staff tour with the County
Clean Water staff review stormwater best management practices

parts.title: FEMA update
presented: FEMA is shifting toward long-term recovery with the County, covering community planning, natural and cultural resources, health and social services, housing, infrastructure and economy.
The application period for FEMA Individual Assistance ends December 11; late applicants with a reason can still apply.
The SBA confirmed a 45-day grace period for loan applications.

parts.title: Questions: cleanup costs, soil results, lead testing, results posting

raised.concern: Asked what percentage the Army Corps charges to manage contracts and why it was used instead of other military engineering agencies that charge less.
Said officials walked Lahaina after the fire without proper protective equipment, showing poor protection of public health.
Asked for soil sample results on his lot and objected to rescraping and to hydromulch instead of replacing removed soil.
Asked whether lead testing will be offered island-wide and how people who miss events can get tested.
Asked where soil and air test results, including FEMA's Lahaina air monitoring data, will be posted publicly.
Said blood lead testing may come too late and suggested urine or hair testing instead.
Asked what the next steps are for building permits for people whose homes burned.
Described a gulch along Haleakalā Highway with a downed utility line, a broken water line, a cable tied to a guardrail, a tree on a pole and a blocked culvert that could flood the highway.
Neighbors of burned lots face contaminated soil and ash but FEMA has denied help; asked which agency will take responsibility.

answered.who: Army Corps Recovery Field Office commander
answered.said: The percentage varies by district and program; the Corps works on FEMA's behalf and he would have to check the figure.
The Corps has been effective and its costs are in line with other disasters; the federal government covers 100% of debris removal, so residents pay nothing beyond turning over any debris insurance.
The Governor chose the Corps; the alternative was the County paying up front and waiting years for reimbursement. The Corps hires local subcontractors, including a Maui company.
He wore a mask off camera and agreed many things could have been done better at the start.
Search and rescue air monitoring showed no hazardous materials in the air when walking on streets, and he offered to share the data.

answered.who: Army Corps Recovery Field Office commander
answered.said: Three of 14 sampled lots need another 6-inch scrape; the Corps will talk with each owner and is working with the County and FEMA on a possible waiver.
Waivers are being drafted, including one for hydromulch, and the Corps will follow up with affected owners.
Screening is offered here tonight and next week and is being scheduled in Lahaina; people can also ask their own health care provider for a lead test.
Results always go on the department's website; a press release with a link will be sent once the new results are analyzed.
Arsenic leaves the body quickly but lead does not, so lead is the right indicator of cumulative exposure and now is an appropriate time to test.
Building permits are not under MEMA's purview and there is no update yet.
The air monitoring data was given to the Maui Police Department, and FEMA can retrieve and provide it.
Asked for the culvert location so infrastructure staff can track it, and offered to coordinate Team Rubicon volunteers for debris clearing.

next.what: Department of Health press release with link to air sampling results

parts.title: Questions: sampling methods, notifications, lead screening limits, water

raised.concern: Asked what soil sampling tests for and whether it covers volatile organic compounds released by water and disturbance.
Said the Corps had promised to post air quality results, including VOCs, on a public website but they have not appeared.
Asked what the stormwater best management practices are made of.
Asked for the debris call center phone number.
Said promised door-to-door notices of neighbors' cleanup schedules never happened.
Said blood screening misses ongoing lower-level exposure while people, including those outside the burn area, are getting sick.
Thanked the Department of Health for lead screening and for alerting doctors, and said cleanup on her street has been well controlled.
A water system defect on a Kula street can shut off water to many homes, leaving no water for firefighting; a tank that once covered it is gone.
Reviewed the timeline since August 8 and said neighbors living next to arsenic-contaminated lots still have no resources.
Asked what contaminants were in the water supply after the fire and their possible health effects.

answered.said: Lots are tested for 16 metals against Hawaiʻi action levels; waste characterization found metals were the issue, and she will follow up with details on VOCs.
Specialists are still reviewing and validating results by parcel; she has no date for posting but will follow up.
Wattles are placed around storm drains and fencing is used to keep ash and soil on site; she will follow up on the materials.
The debris call center number is 877-214-9117, also listed on MauiRecovery.org.

answered.who: Army Corps Recovery Field Office commander
answered.said: Community input led to street sweepers for dust and to sharing updated schedules with the County for neighbor notices.
Apologized, said these are improvements still to make, and promised door hangers and better daily emails.
Lead is a screening indicator of cumulative ash exposure for people without symptoms; people with symptoms should see their health care provider for evaluation.
Offered to meet after the meeting to see the photos.
The department did not test the water; that is the County's responsibility.

next.what: Army Corps follow-up on VOC testing, air results posting and barrier materials

parts.title: Closing
presented: Officials stayed after the meeting for one-on-one questions.

open_questions.question: What percentage does the Army Corps charge to manage the Maui debris removal contracts?
Which agency will help neighbors of burned lots whose soil and ash may be contaminated?
When will the Army Corps air quality and VOC results be posted publicly?
What are the next steps for building permits for Kula homeowners?
What contaminants were in Upcountry tap water after the fire, and what are the health effects?
Will the water system defect that can cut off firefighting water on a Kula street be fixed?
